rv.q: For the first time in my experience, this show is really elfin’ good.
The production is a winner in its most vital pursuit: getting children to laugh.
It's a tonic of a performance — the kind that makes you smile later, just thinking about it.

The updated Elf remains as much a mixed bag as it was during its previous two Broadway stagings in 2010 and 2012, with one major improvement: Grey Henson, the immensely likable, pitched-to-the-rafters firecracker from Mean Girls and Shucked, steps as easily into Buddy’s green winklepickers as Cinderella ever did a glass slilpper.
The result is a rare thing: a musical comedy based on a contemporary hit movie that succeeds on its own giddy ingenuity.

Elf: The Musical passes an important test of a seasonal Broadway show. It passes the wide smile/slightly moistened eyes/ridiculous amount of falling snow test, and—more significantly—passes the far more difficult actually-not-annoying-for-kids-and-adults test.
Go, and I can pretty much guarantee you will have yourself a grand "sparklejollytwinklejingley" time.
It made this jaded critic believe in Santa Claus again for one glimmering, ephemeral moment of theater magic.
For subversively funny delight, suitable for knowing adult and innocent child alike, Elf on Broadway makes a perfect stocking-stuffer.
'Elf the Musical' will likely please the fans of its cinematic predecessor.

But this latest production — overlong,, more dopey than witty, and mostly missing the spark of the original — largely demonstrates that, sometimes, Christmas spirit is not enough to keep a vehicle aloft.
I am delighted to shout to the chimney tops that I was wrong.
'Tis the season when you should stop quibbling for perfection and instead let the holiday spirit envelop you like a warm hug from an oversize elf.

cn.t: This cheerful revival delivers crowd-pleasing holiday fun with Grey Henson's charming lead performance and dazzling production design, though critics note the score remains forgettable and the comedy can be clunky.

sg.ra: The Marquis is the only Broadway house built entirely inside a hotel (3rd floor of the Marriott Marquis), so the orchestra was engineered from scratch in 1986 with a gentle continuous rake and no interior columns. Center Orchestra rows C-H deliver the theater's signature payoff: Portman designed every seat to be within 80 ft of the stage, so even at row F you are close enough to read faces, with none of the pre-war pillars or sightline quirks of older 46th Street houses. Aisle seats gain from the above-average legroom the hotel footprint allows.

Because the Marquis sits inside the hotel's structural envelope, the proscenium is 40 ft wide but wings are only 20 ft — half code. That unusually shallow stage means side-orchestra patrons lose less upstage action than they would at a wider house; what gets cut is limited to the far corner opposite your seat. Double-digit seats in the Right Orchestra are explicitly noted as giving partial views of the stage-right corner, so shows with heavy blocking at the edges (spectacle musicals) still work here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang but it barely bites
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang technically begins at Orchestra row M, but multiple source guides agree the Marquis overhang is unusually forgiving — a quirk of the 1986 hotel-integrated design where Portman's 80-ft max-distance rule kept the balcony pulled forward but shallow. Reviewers consistently report the stage itself remains clearly visible even in the back rows, and the rear orchestra prices drop to a mid tier while you keep the same smooth rake. The real tradeoff here is detail/immersion, not obstruction. Accessible (Row Y) seating is in this zone via ramp.

sg.vl: Row A is a premium orchestra alternative
sg.ra: The Marquis mezzanine is the theater's signature asset: because the house was built fresh in 1986 inside the hotel shell rather than retrofitted, designers used true stadium stepping with a 'gap' between rows so the person in front of you does not block sightlines. Reviewers and Tripadvisor users repeatedly single out Row A Center Mezz as sometimes preferable to any orchestra seat — elevated, unobstructed, pulled forward by the 80-ft rule. Front-mezz single-digit seats deliver the sweeping view musicals are meant to be seen from.

The Marquis mezzanine only runs 12 rows deep (A-M, no I) — shallow by Broadway standards because the hotel footprint capped balcony depth. That means row H is still close to the stage by mezzanine math, and the stadium stepping holds all the way back. Rows H-K near center are flagged as good value across multiple guides: single-digit seats clear the rail, the elevated angle still suits musicals, and prices drop meaningfully versus rows A-D.

Two Marquis-specific drawbacks converge here. First, the NYTix venue guide notes 'rear mezz audio is sometimes a bit fuzzy as are the sight lines from this area' — consistent with BWW forum complaints that the Marquis has unusually dead natural acoustics because the carpeted hotel-interior walls absorb sound. Second, mezzanine access is stairs-only from the lobby (no elevator to this level), so the cheapest seats are also the hardest to reach. Far-side mezz seats additionally lose the corresponding stage corner.

vr.q: I thoroughly recommend the show for a good holiday treat I laughed a lot I had a great time it was really fun it was a spectacle as well just a great show
I didn't realize how much I need the holidays to start a little early this year until I saw Elf on Broadway, and this was an absolute delight from beginning to end.
Call me Scrooge but I didn't like this — but I can see why other people do. I thought the story was tired and the music was generic, but I guess it was fun for what it was.
